items.title: Don't reuse connection pool for SQLite `:memory:` databases
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes #59028

Calling `ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection` twice with the same SQLite `:memory:` config returns the existing pool, because the handler reuses a pool whenever the `db_config` is equal. The second call is meant to describe a new database, but it gets the first one back.

`ConnectionHandling#establish_connection` now passes `clobber: true` to the connection handler when it is given a Hash config for a SQLite `:memory:` database. The handler already supports `clobber`: it disconnects the existing
pool, installs a new one and instruments `!connection.active_record`, so no handler changes are needed.

The rule is limited to the public `establish_connection` entry point on purpose:

* Named configs (`establish_connection(:arunit)`, env names) keep reusing their pool. The test suite re-establishes `:arunit` in many setups and teardowns and relies on this. Under `ARCONN=sqlite3_mem`, a fresh pool there would mean an empty, schema-less database.
* `connects_to` goes through the handler directly and is unchanged. The fixtures' `!connection.active_record` subscriber re-runs `setup_shared_connection_pool` whenever a pool is built, so building fresh pools there would change how shared reading/writing pools behave in tests (e.g. `ShardsKeysTest`).

The test uses a dedicated abstract class rather than `ActiveRecord::Base`, so the suite's own connection is never replaced.

### Additional information

Not covered: a String URL such as `"sqlite3::memory:"`, since at this point a String can't be told apart from a named config. Happy to extend this if reviewers think it's worth it.

items.title: Don't parenthesize an ordered CTE term in a UNION on SQLite
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes #59706

A `with_recursive` whose recursive term carries an `ORDER BY` generated invalid SQL on SQLite:

```ruby
Post.with_recursive(
  post_and_replies: [
    Post.where(id: 42),
    Post.joins("JOIN post_and_replies ON posts.in_reply_to_id = post_and_replies.id").order(:id)
  ]
).load
```

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE "post_and_replies" AS (
  SELECT "posts".* FROM "posts" WHERE "posts"."id" = ?
  UNION ALL
  (SELECT "posts".* FROM "posts" JOIN post_and_replies ON ... ORDER BY "posts"."id" ASC)
) SELECT "posts".* FROM "posts"
```

SQLite does not allow parentheses around a compound-select operand, so this raised `ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid: SQLite3::SQLException: near "(": syntax error`. `ORDER BY` in a recursive term is valid SQLite and controls depth-first vs breadth-first order (https://sqlite.org/lang_with.html).

### Detail

The SQLite visitor already intends to leave UNION operands unparenthesized (that is why it exists), but it rendered each operand through `grouping_parentheses(..., always_wrap_selects: false)`, and that still wraps a `SELECT` whose `require_parentheses?` is true (non-empty orders, a limit, or an offset). Visiting the operand directly leaves it unwrapped, which is the only valid form on SQLite. Simple operands are unchanged (they were never wrapped).

### Additional information

Added a regression test (`test_with_recursive_with_ordered_term`) that loads a recursive CTE with an ordered recursive term; it errors before this change and passes after. Other adapters already accept the parenthesized form, so they are unaffected.

items.title: Find SQLite tables by any ASCII case of their name in the schema readers
items.body:
Stacked on #59668, which should merge first; only the last commit (`9bf31a08d7`) is new here.

2cb3daba96 batched the SQLite schema readers, which now match table names exactly. The previous pragma-based readers matched them the way SQLite does, ignoring ASCII case. So a model whose `table_name` is `"widgets"` can no longer read a table created as `Widgets`: `columns` and `primary_key` raise `StatementInvalid`, and indexes and foreign keys come back empty. ransack's [`context_spec.rb`](https://github.com/activerecord-hackery/ransack/blob/fbc3baf164da2a80435d5678a77924c66472f694/spec/ransack/active_record/context_spec.rb#L73-L81) hits this.

The readers now match with `COLLATE NOCASE`, which folds only ASCII, like SQLite identifiers, so `Ärger` and `ärger` stay two tables. A table read with a different ASCII-case spelling also gets its collations and auto-increment, which 8-1-stable lost. #59668's check that lets a temporary table or view hide a permanent one is now case-insensitive as well.

items.title: Quote `Rational` values as floats
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

`Rational#to_s` returns a fraction, so `quote(Rational(1, 2))` produces `1/2`. PostgreSQL and SQLite evaluate that with integer division, so the value silently becomes `0`:

```ruby
# SQLite, prepared_statements: false
Item.create!(price: 0.25)
Item.where("price < ?", Rational(1, 2)).count # => 0, expected 1
Item.sanitize_sql_array(["price < ?", Rational(1, 2)]) # => "price < 1/2"
```

This affects every path that quotes values into the SQL rather than binding them: unprepared statements, `sanitize_sql_array`, and `connection.quote`.

### Detail

#44404 fixed this for MySQL by casting bound Rationals with `to_f`. The PostgreSQL and SQLite adapters' `type_cast` methods already use `to_f` for bind parameters. This applies the same conversion in the abstract `quote`, so quoted and bound Rationals agree on every adapter.

The existing PostgreSQL and SQLite tests asserting `"3/4"` and `"0/1"` were updated. They were brought over from the MySQL tests and recorded the previous output rather than an intended behavior.

### Additional information

`to_f` can lose precision for some Rationals. This matches the existing MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQLite bind behavior, and is closer to the intended value than integer division.

items.title: Fix SQLite boolean column defaults for overridden attribute types
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes #58292.

`extract_value_from_default` returned actual Ruby `true` / `false` objects for `DEFAULT TRUE` / `DEFAULT FALSE` literals, unlike every other branch in that method, which returns a `String`.

This pre-cast value became the attribute's `value_before_type_cast`, so overriding a boolean column with:

```ruby
attribute :name, :integer
```

fed a Ruby boolean directly into `Integer#deserialize`, raising:

```text
NoMethodError: undefined method `to_i' for true
```

This is a residual gap in `fb04401a66` ("Stop deserializing column defaults"), which fixed the general column-default double-casting issue behind #58292 but reintroduced the same failure specifically for SQLite's `TRUE` / `FALSE` literal parsing.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes SQLite boolean default extraction to return `"1"` / `"0"` strings instead of Ruby `true` / `false` objects.

This matches the plain-scalar contract of the other branches in `extract_value_from_default` and restores the pre-8.1 behavior where the column default round-trips through the overriding type correctly.

Regression coverage verifies that:

* a boolean schema default can be read through an overridden integer attribute type; and
* a non-boolean integer value can still be written and reloaded through the overridden attribute.

### Additional information

MySQL / Trilogy already return plain numeric strings for `tinyint(1)` defaults and are unaffected by this regression.

PostgreSQL already returns the literal `"true"` / `"false"` string, rather than a cast Ruby `Boolean`, from its own `extract_value_from_default`, so it is not affected by this particular regression.

PostgreSQL has separate, longstanding limitations with overriding native boolean columns with non-boolean attribute types. Those behaviors predate this regression and are outside the scope of this change.

items.title: SQLite table reconstruction cascade-deletes child rows inside transac…
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

SQLite does not allow `PRAGMA foreign_keys` to be changed while a transaction is active.
Although the SQLite adapter disables referential integrity before rebuilding a table,
`ActiveRecord::Migrator` has already opened an outer DDL transaction by that point.
Consequently, disabling foreign keys is a no-op and dropping the original table during
reconstruction can trigger `ON DELETE CASCADE`, silently deleting rows from referencing
tables.

Fixes #58705.

### Detail

This pull request introduces an adapter hook for migration transactions. The default
implementation preserves the existing transaction behavior, while SQLite overrides the
hook to disable referential integrity before opening the migration transaction and restore
it afterward.

The regression test runs the schema change through `MigrationContext`, verifies that
referencing rows survive the table reconstruction, and confirms that foreign key
enforcement and cascading deletes still work after the migration completes.

items.title: Reset connections reclaimed from worker Ractors before checkin
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

When a worker Ractor exits without releasing its connection token, a supervisor can reclaim it with `RactorConnectionHandler::Proxy.checkin_all_connections`. This currently returns the connection to its pool without resetting an open transaction. The next borrower can inherit the worker's unfinished transaction and uncommitted writes.

This follows up on #59119, which keeps the proxied transaction state on the main Ractor. It applies directly to Rails main.

### Detail

Match `ConnectionPool#reap` when reclaiming these connections: reset active connections before checking them in, and remove inactive connections from the pool.

Add regression tests for an abandoned transaction and a disconnected connection. The transaction test fails before the fix because `open_transactions` remains 1 after cleanup; after the fix it is 0 and the uncommitted row is absent.

items.title: Disconnect when a thread is killed during configure_connection
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

When a thread is killed with `Thread#kill` while Active Record sets up a new connection's session (`configure_connection`), and the thread returns the connection to the pool on its way out, the next thread that checks the connection out runs on a session that was never fully set up. On PostgreSQL every query on that connection then raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'key?' for nil` (the result type map was never loaded). On SQLite the pragmas are SQLite's defaults, so foreign keys are not enforced and the journal is not WAL. Nothing raises on SQLite. It lasts until the connection is reconnected.

#54711 made `attempt_configure_connection` disconnect the adapter when setup fails, and #54738 widened its `rescue` to `Exception` so `Timeout.timeout` is covered too. A killed thread skips `rescue` and runs only `ensure` blocks, so the adapter keeps its raw connection and stays marked as verified. Returning the connection is ordinary: `with_connection` does it in an `ensure`, and so does the executor at the end of a request or job.

Threads get killed while the process goes on using the pool, for example:

- the parallel gem's `in_threads` kills its worker threads when its caller is interrupted, e.g. by a request timeout,
- job workers built on `Concurrent::ThreadPoolExecutor` kill threads still running after their shutdown timeout, and Puma kills them after `force_shutdown_after`. Here the pool is only used again if the process keeps running.

What keeps a thread in session setup is a database that is slow to answer at that moment.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction (fails on main, passes on this branch)</summary>

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main"
  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record"
require "tmpdir"

database = File.join(Dir.mktmpdir, "development.sqlite3")
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: database, pool: 1, timeout: 5000)
pool = ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool

# Another process holds the write lock (a migration, a backup), so session
# setup waits in `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL`.
blocker = SQLite3::Database.new(database)
blocker.execute("BEGIN EXCLUSIVE")

request = Thread.new do
  pool.with_connection { |connection| connection.select_value("SELECT 1") }
end
sleep 0.01 until request.backtrace&.any? { |line| line.match?(/[#`]configure_connection'/) }
request.kill.join # an app server or job worker stopping after its shutdown timeout
blocker.execute("ROLLBACK")

pool.with_connection do |connection|
  puts "journal_mode=#{connection.select_value("PRAGMA journal_mode")} " \
    "foreign_keys=#{connection.select_value("PRAGMA foreign_keys")}"
end
```

On main:

```
journal_mode=delete foreign_keys=0
```

On this branch:

```
journal_mode=wal foreign_keys=1
```

</details>

### Detail

This Pull Request moves the cleanup in `attempt_configure_connection` from a `rescue Exception` to an `ensure`, which disconnects unless the block completed. It still returns the block's value. It also disconnects when the block is left by `throw` or a non-local `return`, which nothing in Rails does today.

### Additional information

The test kills a thread inside `configure_connection` and checks that the next query on the connection sets the session up again. It fails without the change on SQLite and PostgreSQL. The Active Record suite passes on SQLite and PostgreSQL; MySQL was not run, but the change is in `AbstractAdapter`, which the MySQL adapters share.

I also reproduced this with a real PostgreSQL server made slow by a proxy, with `with_connection` on main, 8.1.4.1, 8.0.5.2, 7.2.4 and 7.1.6, and with a release in an `ensure` on main and 8.1.4.1. On main I also tried a `Concurrent::ThreadPoolExecutor` job worker that is shut down and then killed, and the parallel gem under `Timeout.timeout`; both fail the same way. Puma's forced shutdown was only tried with a second server in the same process, which isn't how Puma restarts. A thread that leases a connection and never returns it is not affected: the reaper resets it.

#59567 also changes `attempt_configure_connection`. The two changes don't overlap in behaviour, but whichever lands second needs a small rebase.

items.title: Fix SQLite `db:reset` silently discarding schema on single-env apps
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

With a single-environment `database.yml` (only `development`, no `test`), `bin/rails db:reset` — or `db:drop db:create db:schema:load` — left the recreated database empty: queries raised `no such table`. Reported by @rosa on behalf of @joemasilotti (#53832), reproducible with the app at rosa/phantom-db-sqlite-repro.

### Detail

`check_protected_environments!` runs before `drop` and establishes/caches a connection pool for the single `db_config`. `SQLiteDatabaseTasks#drop` removed the database file but did **not** disconnect, so the connection handler's `establish_connection` short-circuit returned that stale pool to the following `create`/`schema:load`, which wrote to the deleted file's inode instead of the recreated file. With both `development` and `test` configured the bug is hidden, because switching db_configs disconnects between tasks.

`drop` now disconnects the dropped database's own pool(s) before removing the file, so `create` reconnects to the new file. Only SQLite pools for the database being dropped are disconnected (not the global connection, so `db:drop:all` never closes an unrelated database or a different adapter with the same database name), and in-memory databases are skipped (they have no file and would lose their data).

This revives #53893 by @rosa (approach approved by @rafaelfranca). The original two-line fix disconnected the global connection unconditionally, which broke the `sqlite3_mem` suite; the per-database, in-memory-guarded disconnect avoids that.

### Additional information

Four regression tests in the SQLite rake tests:
- `drop` + `create` persists the schema to the recreated file (fails before the fix);
- `drop` of a configured-but-never-opened database does not recreate the file and still reports it as missing;
- dropping one database does not disconnect a different, live connection (fails against the previous global-connection approach);
- dropping a SQLite database does not disconnect a different adapter's pool with the same database name (fails before the adapter guard).

With Ruby 3.4.8 and `RAILS_STRICT_WARNINGS=1`, the full Active Record SQLite suites pass: `test:sqlite3` — 9,851 runs, 35,134 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors; `test:sqlite3_mem` — 9,647 runs, 33,857 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors. RuboCop reports no offenses in the changed Ruby files. Other database adapters were not run locally because the change is SQLite-specific. Fixes #53832.

items.title: Preserve the worker pool in Ractor checkout errors
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

When a worker Ractor cannot check out a connection from an exhausted pool, its `ConnectionTimeoutError.connection_pool` is `nil`. items.title: Preserve the lock when re-pinning a Ractor connection
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

`ProxyConnectionPool#pin_connection!(true)` replaces the worker-side adapter's lock on every call. A nested pin therefore installs a different lock from the one an outer pin established. Threads using the same proxy adapter can then synchronize against different lock objects.

The regular connection pool already preserves the lock after #59045; the Ractor proxy still uses the previous behavior.

### Detail

Install a worker-side lock only when locking is requested and the connection currently uses `NullLock`, matching `ConnectionPool#pin_connection!`.

items.title: Preserve existing leases across nested with_connection in Ractors
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

In a worker Ractor, calling `lease_connection` inside an outer `with_connection` block should keep the connection checked out after that block ends. items.title: Respect checkout timeouts in worker Ractors

items.title: Honor an overridden primary_key method in relation finders
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes #59622

`primary_key` is documented as overridable in subclasses, and before `ActiveRecord::PrimaryKey` was introduced (55406a9794) relation finders used it directly, so an override took effect.

Now finders (`Model.all.find`, `Model.all.find([ids])`, …) build their condition from `primary_key_definition`, which is resolved from the schema. A class that overrides the `primary_key` class method is therefore ignored by relation finders: the condition uses the schema-derived key — an empty column name when the table has no primary key — so the query fails:

```
main:        SELECT "menu_items".* FROM "menu_items" WHERE "menu_items"."" = ? LIMIT ?
8-1-stable:  SELECT "menu_items".* FROM "menu_items" WHERE "menu_items"."uuid_key" = ? LIMIT ?
```

`Model.find(id)` still works, which is what masks it. This is a regression on `main` only (8-1-stable is correct); friendly_id's `UuidAsPrimaryKeyFindTest` hits it.

```ruby
class MenuItem < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.table_name = "menu_items" # id: false, with a uuid_key column
  def self.primary_key
    "uuid_key"
  end
end

MenuItem.primary_key        # => "uuid_key"
MenuItem.all.find("abc")    # main: ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid (no such column: menu_items.)
```

### Detail

In `load_primary_key_definition`, after resolving the inherited/schema definition, rebuild `primary_key_definition` from the overridden `primary_key` value when the `primary_key` class method is overridden. Every consumer of `primary_key_definition` (relation finders, associations, counter cache, …) then honors the override.

### Motivation / Background

Rejecting an isolation-level change inside an open transaction currently clears the pool's existing isolation setting. The validation raises before `old_level` is assigned, but `ensure` still restores that uninitialized local as `nil`.

items.title: Release tokens for invalidated Ractor connection leases
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

After the main connection pool calls `disconnect!`, a worker's leased proxy no longer holds a main-side connection. `ProxyConnectionPool#connection_lease` notices this and clears the local lease, but leaves its token in `Proxy.connections`, retaining the old connection.

The stale token remains even when the worker explicitly releases its connection. Checking out again adds a new token alongside the old one, so repeated invalidation and checkout can accumulate disconnected adapters in the registry.

### Detail

Release the proxy adapter's token before clearing an invalidated lease. The existing token release path removes the registry entry and only checks the real connection in if it is still in use.

Add regressions for reacquiring a connection after a main-pool disconnect and explicitly releasing an invalidated lease from a worker Ractor. Both fail before the fix: reacquisition leaves tokens `[1, 2]` instead of `[2]`, and release leaves the old registry entry. The tests also check that the previous proxy loses its token and the replacement can execute a query.

items.title: Batch over several columns with a row value comparison
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because batching over several columns (a composite primary key, or a multi-column `cursor:`) gets slower with every batch on PostgreSQL and SQLite.

```ruby
class Event < ApplicationRecord
  self.primary_key = [:tenant_id, :id]
end

Event.find_each { |event| ... }
```

Every batch after the first asks for the rows after the cursor with:

```sql
WHERE ("events"."tenant_id" > 50 OR "events"."tenant_id" = 50 AND "events"."id" > 500000)
ORDER BY "events"."tenant_id" ASC, "events"."id" ASC LIMIT 1000
```

PostgreSQL and SQLite can only use that as a filter: they read the primary key index from its start, so each batch reads again every row before it and walking a table is quadratic. Written as a row value comparison,

```sql
WHERE ("events"."tenant_id", "events"."id") > (50, 500000)
```

they start reading the index at the cursor. Halfway through a million rows, the next batch on PostgreSQL goes from 4,081 index pages to 13.

### Detail

Batches use a row value comparison when the adapter says, through a new private `supports_row_value_comparison?`, that it reads an index from one (PostgreSQL and SQLite), and every cursor column goes in the same order. Otherwise the condition is unchanged: that covers mixed orders and MySQL, which [uses an index for the current condition and not for row values](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/row-constructor-optimization.html). Single-column cursors don't change, and there is no new public API.

Types that compare through an expression (`ActiveRecord::Type::QueryPredicates`) get it on both sides, as in `(lower(title), id) > (lower('a'), 1)`.

On PostgreSQL before 18 the condition also repeats the first column's bound, `tenant_id >= 50 AND (tenant_id, id) > (50, 500000)`. Without it, a relation with an `IN` list on that column (`Event.where(tenant_id: [10, 50, 90]).find_each`) scans from the list's first value up to the cursor on PostgreSQL 14 to 17. PostgreSQL 18 doesn't need it, and there it would make the ranges `in_batches` yields read on to the end of the first column's value.

### Additional information

Walking a million rows with a `(tenant_id, id)` primary key, `main` → this branch (Ryzen 3 PRO 4450U on AC power, mean of two runs):

| | `in_batches(of: 1000) { }` | `find_each { }` | Next batch, halfway |
|---|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL 16 | 35.1 s → 0.9 s | 89.8 s → 22.8 s | 70 ms → 5.7 ms |
| PostgreSQL 17 | 34.8 s → 0.9 s | 92.6 s → 22.7 s | 81 ms → 6.3 ms |
| PostgreSQL 18 | 32.6 s → 0.9 s | 93.6 s → 22.8 s | 74 ms → 6.1 ms |
| SQLite 3.54 | 48.7 s → 0.3 s | 45.1 s → 22.4 s | 27 ms → 5.7 ms |

A `cursor: [:created_at, :id]` improves as well, even with an index on `created_at` alone (3,770 → 12 pages on PostgreSQL). With an `IN` list on the first column, `find_each` takes the same as on `main`.

Index pages read by the next batch (`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`, 1,000 × 1,000 rows, cursor halfway). The condition this branch uses is in bold; PostgreSQL 14 and 15 match 16.

| Condition | PostgreSQL 16 | PostgreSQL 17 | PostgreSQL 18 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`find_each`** | | | |
| `OR` (`main`) | 1369 | 1369 | 1369 |
| Row value | 7 | 7 | **7** |
| Row value with the repeated bound | **7** | **7** | 7 |
| **`where(author_id: [100, 500, 900]).find_each`** | | | |
| `OR` (`main`) | 17 | 17 | 19 |
| Row value | 1107 | 1102 | **19** |
| Row value with the repeated bound | **12** | **12** | 13 |
| **A range yielded by `in_batches`** | | | |
| `OR` (`main`) | 3589 | 3588 | 3588 |
| Row value | 279 | 279 | **7** |
| Row value with the repeated bound | **279** | **279** | 279 |

<details>
<summary>Benchmark script</summary>

```ruby
#   RAILS_PATH=/path/to/rails ADAPTER=postgresql DATABASE_URL=postgres://... ruby bench_batches.rb
#   RAILS_PATH=/path/to/rails ADAPTER=sqlite3 ruby bench_batches.rb
require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true, quiet: true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"
  gem "rails", path: ENV.fetch("RAILS_PATH")
  gem "pg"
  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record"

ROWS = Integer(ENV.fetch("ROWS", "1000000"))
postgres = ENV.fetch("ADAPTER") == "postgresql"
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(postgres ? ENV.fetch("DATABASE_URL") : { adapter: "sqlite3", database: "/tmp/bench_batches.sqlite3" })
ActiveRecord::Base.logger = nil
conn = ActiveRecord::Base.lease_connection

ActiveRecord::Schema.verbose = false
ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :events, primary_key: [:tenant_id, :id], force: true do |t|
    t.integer :tenant_id, null: false
    t.integer :id, null: false
    t.string :name
  end
end

class Event < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.primary_key = [:tenant_id, :id]
end

# 100 tenants with ROWS / 100 events each.
series = postgres ? "generate_series(0, #{ROWS - 1}) AS s(g)" : "(WITH RECURSIVE s(g) AS (SELECT 0 UNION ALL SELECT g + 1 FROM s WHERE g < #{ROWS - 1}) SELECT g FROM s) AS s"

puts "in_batches: #{time.() { Event.in_batches(of: 1000) { } }.round(2)} s"
```

items.title: Fix SQLite schema dump for multiline virtual tables, generated columns, and collations
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes #58123. Fixes #58131.

SQLite's schema regexes assume single-line DDL, but SQLite stores the `CREATE` statement in `sqlite_master` verbatim, newlines and all. Write the DDL multiline (the natural way with a heredoc in a migration) and the introspection break in two ways that've been reported:

- #58123: `bin/rails db:schema:dump` crashes with `NoMethodError: undefined   method 'split' for nil` on a multiline `CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE` (like an FTS5   table). `VIRTUAL_TABLE_REGEX` doesn't match, so the capture comes back `nil`. 
- #58131: multiline `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...)` columns and `COLLATE` clauses are  *silently* dropped. `db/schema.rb` reloads with `as: nil` (a permanently-NULL column) and missing collations. No crash, just quiet corruption.

#56969 did fix the empty-parens case on this same regex. This PR fixes the multiline issue.

### Detail

Normalise the stored SQL with `squish` before matching, rather than only adding the `m` flag.

Adding `m` _does_ stop the crash, but the captured args keep their newlines, so the dumper's `arguments.split(", ")` never splits and you get a mess:

```ruby
create_virtual_table "search", "fts5", ["\n  title,\n  body,\n  tokenize='...'\n"]
```

`squish` collapses the whitespace first, so the dump comes out identical to the single-line form:

```ruby
create_virtual_table "search", "fts5", ["title", "body", "tokenize='porter unicode61'"]
```

For generated columns and collations there's a second bug behind #58131: the column split in `table_structure_sql` only allowed a single whitespace char after the comma, so indented DDL never split and the whole table body came back as one chunk. Only the first column's collation/expression could be captured, which is why a second collated column silently lost its `COLLATE`. Changing `\s` to `\s+` fixes the split, and `squish` on each column string then lets the existing regexes match.

### Additional information

One trade-off: `squish` collapses whitespace inside string literals too. In practice that only matters for a literal with repeated spaces inside a generated expression or FTS5 option, which I've not hit in real schemas. Happy to switch to the narrower `m`-flag plus arg-normalisation if you'd rather keep literals byte-for-byte.

I did add a CHANGELOG entry since this changes what actually gets dumped, not just the crash. Happy to drop if the doesn't meet the guidelines but I was a bit unclear.

Tests cover all cases from both issues: multiline virtual table, multiline
generated column, and multiple collated columns. `rubocop` is clean.

`while_preventing_writes` classified a query by its first keyword only, so a query starting with `WITH` or `SELECT` could still write:

```sql
SELECT 1 LIMIT 1; UPDATE users SET name = 'x'
```

* multiple statements (`;` followed by another statement), and
* data-modifying statements (`INSERT` / `UPDATE` / `DELETE`) hiding inside a common table expression.

String literals, quoted identifiers and comments are stripped before scanning, so keywords and semicolons inside them are not mistaken for SQL — e.g. `SELECT * FROM t WHERE nick = 'a;b'` and `-- DELETE ...\nSELECT ...` still pass.

items.title: Fix encrypted_attribute? for binary columns on PostgreSQL
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because `encrypted_attribute?` always returns `false` for a persisted, encrypted binary (`bytea`) attribute on PostgreSQL, and `ciphertext_for` returns a freshly encrypted value rather than the stored ciphertext.

```ruby
class Book < ActiveRecord::Base
  encrypts :logo # t.binary :logo
end

book = Book.find(Book.create!(logo: "Dune").id)

book.encrypted_attribute?(:logo)
# PostgreSQL: false
# SQLite, MySQL: true

book.ciphertext_for(:logo)
# PostgreSQL: a newly encrypted value, not the one stored in the database
```

PostgreSQL returns `bytea` values in their escaped form (e.g. `\x7b2270...`), so `EncryptedAttributeType#encrypted?` tries to parse the escaped string as an encrypted message and fails. `ciphertext_for` then falls back to `read_attribute_for_database`, which encrypts the value again. Records that have only just been saved aren't affected, because they still hold the unescaped value in memory, so the problem only shows up once a record is loaded from the database.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes `EncryptedAttributeType#encrypted?` to decode the value with `database_type_to_text` before checking it, as `deserialize` already does. Text columns are unaffected, since `database_type_to_text` returns their value unchanged.

On PostgreSQL, `ciphertext_for` on a binary attribute now returns the persisted value as read from the database, i.e. in its escaped form, matching `read_attribute_before_type_cast` as it already does for text columns. This value still decrypts with `type_for_attribute(name).deserialize`.

### Additional information

I found this while planning to encrypt an existing `bytea` column in place and wanting to use `encrypted_attribute?` to skip rows that had already been encrypted.

The new tests fail on PostgreSQL without this change and pass with it. On SQLite and MySQL they pass either way, as those adapters return binary values as raw bytes. I ran the encryption tests against PostgreSQL, SQLite, and MariaDB (with both mysql2 and trilogy), and the full Active Record suite against PostgreSQL.

This Pull Request has been created because `save` returns `true` when a `before_commit` callback rolls the implicit transaction back with `ActiveRecord::Rollback`. items.title: Avoid quadratic lookups when replacing a collection association
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Replacing a collection association calls `Array#index` once for every record shared
by the old and the new target. Each call scans the target from the start, so
replacing a collection of n records costs `O(n**2)` comparisons.

This shows up when assigning a large collection, and in Active Storage when adding
a file to an existing `has_many_attached` collection, as reported in #50848.
#46652 suggests building a local index instead.

### Detail

`replace_common_records_in_memory` now builds a lookup of the target once and passes
it to `replace_on_target`, which uses it instead of `Array#index`.

The index lives only for that one call. It keeps the first occurrence of equal
records, matching what `Array#index` returns. Replacements assign in place, so
positions do not move, and appends only add after the first matching position, so
the index stays valid for the whole loop.

The lookup relies on Active Record's standard `hash`/`eql?` behavior, which
`intersection` already uses to select the common records, so no new assumption is
introduced. Models that override `==` need to keep `eql?` and `hash` consistent with
it; the `eql?` alias inherited from `ActiveRecord::Core` does not pick up an
override of `==`.

### Additional information

Benchmark for `owner.items = items` on this branch, Ruby 4.0.6 with SQLite, median
of 10 runs after 2 warmups:

| Records | Before | After |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 100 | 5.05 ms | 1.43 ms |
| 1,000 | 381.56 ms | 14.18 ms |

Allocations at 1,000 records: 12,003 before, 12,005 after.

Three tests are added: replacement with equal but distinct instances, a target that
already contains equal records, and adding a new record alongside existing ones. The
second builds the target directly and calls the private method in order to pin down
*which* occurrence is replaced; an index built with `each_with_index.to_h` would keep
the last occurrence, and no other test in the suites listed below catches the
difference. The existing
`NestedThroughAssociationsTest#test_nested_has_many_through_writers_should_raise_error`
also reaches this code with a duplicated target, but its assertions are about
read-only association errors.

The `has_many_associations`, `has_many_through_associations`,
`has_and_belongs_to_many_associations`, `inverse_associations`, and
`nested_through_associations` suites pass with SQLite.

Related: #58533 previously proposed a similar local index for collection
replacement together with an Active Storage attachment lookup optimization.
This PR focuses on the Active Record part and adds regression tests for
replacement behavior.

This partially addresses #50848. The other quadratic lookup, in
`ActiveStorage::Attached::Changes::CreateOneOfMany#find_attachment`, is left for a
separate change.

items.title: Set auto_vacuum=incremental on new SQLite databases and add db:maintenance:vacuum
items.body:
## Summary

SQLite does not return disk space to the OS when rows are deleted. With the default `auto_vacuum=none`, database files grow monotonically regardless of actual data size. This is especially problematic for high-churn databases like Solid Cache, Solid Queue, and Solid Cable — production databases can balloon to many GBs while holding only MBs of real data.

This PR:

- **Sets `auto_vacuum=incremental` on new SQLite databases** — configured in `new_client` before `configure_connection` applies `journal_mode=wal`, because WAL initialization finalizes the database file format after which `auto_vacuum` cannot be changed. Existing databases are unaffected. Users can opt out via `pragmas: { auto_vacuum: none }` in `database.yml`.

- **Introduces `db:maintenance:vacuum` rake task** — runs `PRAGMA incremental_vacuum(1000)` (~4 MB of freed pages) and `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` (resets the WAL file) on all SQLite databases. Warns and skips databases still on `auto_vacuum=none`. Supports per-database variants for multi-DB apps (e.g. `db:maintenance:vacuum:cache`). Non-SQLite databases are skipped automatically.

- **Updates guides** — documents `auto_vacuum` as a creation-time default in the configuring guide, and adds `db:maintenance:vacuum` to the command line guide.

The task is designed to be scheduled (e.g. hourly via Solid Queue recurring tasks). A companion PR to `rails/solid_queue` could add a default entry to `config/recurring.yml` so new apps get this out of the box.

## Why `new_client` instead of `DEFAULT_PRAGMAS`?

`auto_vacuum` is a persistent database property, not a per-connection session pragma. It can only be set on a new, empty database and must be applied **before** `journal_mode=wal` (which initializes the database file format). Setting it in `DEFAULT_PRAGMAS` / `configure_connection` is too late — `journal_mode` runs first and locks in `auto_vacuum=none`. It also fails on readonly and locked connections.

The fix checks `!File.exist?(database)` in `new_client` to detect new databases, sets `auto_vacuum` before returning the raw connection, and lets `configure_connection` proceed normally.

## Context

Rails already sets 6 sensible SQLite defaults (WAL mode, foreign keys, mmap, etc.) but has no protection against unbounded disk growth. Real-world reports:
- [Solid Queue #560](https://github.com/rails/solid_queue/issues/560) — production server ran out of disk space
- [Solid Cache #116](https://github.com/rails/solid_cache/issues/116) — no DB-agnostic way to constrain cache storage size

## Test plan

- [x] `test_create_sets_auto_vacuum_to_incremental_by_default` — new database gets `auto_vacuum=2`
- [x] `test_create_allows_overriding_auto_vacuum_via_pragmas` — user can set `auto_vacuum: none`
- [x] Tests fail without the code change (expects `auto_vacuum=2`, gets `0`)
- [x] Full SQLite adapter suite passes (93 runs, 0 errors)
- [x] Transaction tests pass — no errors on readonly or shared-cache connections (8 runs, 0 errors)
- [x] Full SQLite rake suite passes (19 runs, 0 errors)
- [x] Verified with `rails new --dev` — new databases get `auto_vacuum=2`

items.title: Avoid unnecessary join construction in Relation#eager_loading?
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

`Relation#eager_loading?` is evaluated several times while a query is executed, and `@should_eager_load ||=` does not memoize a `false` result.

When a relation uses `includes` together with `joins`, checking references can build the whole join tree even when no references remain to be checked. This happens both with an empty `references_values` and with references only to the relation's own table, which is already included in the joined-table set. Own-table references are also added by `first`, hash conditions such as `where(posts: ...)`, and ordering such as `order("posts.title")`.

`joined_includes_values` likewise allocates a new array for `includes_values & joins_values` even when either side is empty.

### Detail

* Return `false` from `references_eager_loaded_tables?` immediately when references are empty, or when subtracting the relation's own table leaves no references.
* Otherwise, build the joins and check the remaining references as before. Keep `references_values` unchanged so join alias selection still receives the original references.
* Return `FROZEN_EMPTY_ARRAY` from `joined_includes_values` when `includes_values` or `joins_values` is empty.
* Test both own-table-only references and mixed own/associated-table references, including loaded records and association loading.

For valid joins, the eager-loading decision is unchanged. A direct `eager_loading?` call can now return `false` instead of raising a join validation error when references are empty or contain only the own table. This includes invalid association names, polymorphic joins, and invalid `left_joins` arguments. SQL construction and query execution still raise those errors; `eager_loading?` no longer validates those joins in the fast path.

### Additional information

Fresh measurements comparing the two methods from this PR's parent commit with the updated implementation, using Ruby 4.0.7 without YJIT and SQLite 3.47.2 in memory. The dataset contains one author, two posts, and two comments on the first post. Each iteration builds a fresh relation, with the query cache disabled.

After warming each case for 0.5 seconds, allocations were measured with `GC.stat(:total_allocated_objects)` over 1,000 iterations, repeated five times. Throughput uses `Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` with five 0.5-second samples. The table reports medians. These measurements replace the earlier benchmark numbers and use a different dataset.

Except for the includes-only row, the base relation is `Post.includes(:author).joins(:comments)`.

| Query | Objects/query (Before → After) | Iterations/sec (Before → After) | Ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Base relation, `to_a` | 646 → 382 | 2,667 → 3,569 | 1.34x |
| `Post.includes(:author).to_a` | 313 → 292 | 4,581 → 4,638 | 1.01x |
| Base relation, `first` | 684 → 432 | 2,327 → 3,025 | 1.30x |
| Base relation, `where(posts: { title: "one" }).to_a` | 696 → 444 | 2,311 → 2,934 | 1.27x |
| Base relation, `order("posts.title").to_a` | 692 → 440 | 2,417 → 3,030 | 1.25x |
| Base relation, `to_sql` | 207 → 119 | 12,295 → 18,128 | 1.47x |
| Base relation, `count` | 261 → 173 | 7,095 → 8,700 | 1.23x |

The last row still needs to build joins to check its references. Filtering out the own table adds three objects per reference check; this query performs three checks.

items.title: When joining models across different SQLite databases, automatically ATTACH DATABASE to bring them into scope
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

When using multiple databases you traditionally can't join across databases but SQLite has the unique ability to include different SQLite databases in the connection and treat them one big database. 

Take this setup for example:
```ruby
class ApplicationRecord < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.abstract_class = true
end

class Course < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :entrants
end

class OtherRecord < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.abstract_class = true

  connects_to database: { writing: :other }
end

class Entrant < OtherRecord
  belongs_to :course
end
```

```yaml
default: &default
  adapter: sqlite3

development:
  primary:
    <<: *default
    database: storage/dev.sqlite3
  other:
    <<: *default
    migrations_paths: db/other_migrate
    database: storage/other_dev.sqlite3
```

Prior to this patch if you were to execute `Entrant.joins(:course).where(courses: { name: "Ruby Development" })`, a `StatementInvalid` error will be raised because `Entrant` and `Course` live in different databases. But if you execute `ATTACH DATABASE 'storage/other_dev.sqlite3' as other`, you bring `entrants` into scope and can join over to it. This patch prepends the database name to those external database table calls to avoid conflicts.

Given that we know where these models live, database wise, and SQLite offers us the an avenue to join across databases, we should automatically include those databases into scope and extract that away from the developer when executing a query. 

Since SQLite can be write constrained, if you have a particularly write heavy table, this would allow you to move the table to it's own database and free up the primary database for more writes while still allowing you to treat it as if it was in the primary database. 

### Additional information

[sqlite docs on attach](https://sqlite.org/lang_attach.html)

items.title: Log at info in the test environment of new apps
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because the test environment of a new application logs at the debug level, so every SQL query and every rendered template and partial is written to `log/test.log`. Producing those lines is a large share of the time of a fast test. In a new application with a scaffold, the generated tests spend 15% to 29% of their CPU time on them, and once-campfire's suite spends 4% on them. `production.rb` already reads its level from `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL`; `test.rb` keeps the framework default.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes the generated `config/environments/test.rb` to set:

```ruby
# Logging every SQL query and rendered template at the debug level slows the test suite down.
# Set RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug to log everything.
config.log_level = ENV.fetch("RAILS_LOG_LEVEL", "info")
```

- It is the line `production.rb` has, with a different default. `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug bin/rails test` gives the full log back.
- At the info level `test.log` keeps the request lines (`Started`, `Processing by`, `Completed`), the heading of each test, warnings and errors. It loses the debug lines: SQL, `Rendered …`, the debug lines of Action Mailer and Active Storage, and the unpermitted parameters and strict loading notices, which are logged at debug.
- The event reporter's debug mode follows the log level (`Rails.event.debug_mode = config.log_level.to_s == "debug"`), so in a new application `Rails.event.debug` events reach a test inside `with_debug_event_reporting`, or with `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug`, as in production.
- Existing applications are unchanged unless they take the new `test.rb` from `bin/rails app:update`. The framework default of `config.log_level` stays `:debug`.
- A shared generator test checks the line in the generated application and in a plugin's dummy application. The CHANGELOG has an entry, and the two guides that list the default level per environment now include test.

### Additional information

**Benchmark.** Measured on our machine (laptop, Docker with 4 CPUs, Ruby 3.4.11 +YJIT, SQLite). Two applications generated with `rails new --dev`, one by `main` (a0fd31e1) and one by this branch, with the same `Post` scaffold (32 fixtures) and the same test files, one worker; the arms alternated five times; CPU time of the process from the first test setup, so boot is left out:

| CPU time per test | `main` | this branch | |
|---|---|---|---|
| empty test (2,000 tests) | 298 µs | 222 µs | −25.5%, faster in 5 of 5 rounds |
| one `find` with a fixture (2,000) | 541 µs | 382 µs | −29.3%, 5 of 5 |
| `get posts_url`, 32 rows (300) | 5,022 µs | 3,660 µs | −27.1%, 5 of 5 |
| the scaffold's `posts_controller_test.rb` (7) | 38.5 ms | 32.7 ms | −15.0%, 4 of 5 |

Running this branch's application with `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug` gives `main`'s numbers back (within 4%).

On a real suite, once-campfire (`basecamp/once-campfire` at c8f74a0, on Rails `main`), with its `test.rb` at debug and at info, 536 tests, five rounds: 13.01 s and 12.49 s of CPU time (−4.0%, faster in 4 of 5 rounds), and a `test.log` of 22,198 lines (3.5 MB) and 6,783 lines (0.6 MB) per run. The system tests and eleven test files that open threads or second SQLite connections are left out of this run: in those files the time goes to threads waiting on each other for SQLite locks and the GVL, not to Rails.

<details>
<summary>The test files of the benchmark</summary>

```ruby
class EmptyRailsTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  2000.times { |i| test("t#{i}") { assert true } }
end

class QueryRailsTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  2000.times { |i| test("q#{i}") { assert Post.find(posts(:p1).id) } }
end

class RequestOverheadTest < ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest
  300.times { |i| test("r#{i}") { get posts_url; assert_response :success } }
end
```

The CPU time is read with `Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID)` in the first test's `setup` and in `Minitest.after_run`.

</details>

**Verified.** The new generator test fails on `main` and passes here, for an application and for a plugin's dummy application; five mutations of the template line (level `debug`, another variable, a fixed `:info`, the line commented out, the line removed) each make it fail. The Railties suite passes with `rake test` (2,782 tests in 176 files), apart from six tests that fail the same way on `main` in our container: two IRB colorization tests in `console_test.rb` (no terminal) and four in `sprockets_assets_test.rb` (json 3.0.1 rejects the `create_additions` option that Sprockets 4.2.1 passes). In the two generated applications the scaffold's tests pass at both levels, `test.log` has no SQL or `Rendered` lines at the default level and has them again with `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug`; an `--api` application gets the same line.

**Risk.** Someone who reads `log/test.log` to debug a failing test in a new application no longer finds the SQL there and has to run with `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug`. Reverting the commit restores the previous template.

items.title: SQLite3: Preserve triggers on a table when altering it
items.body:
Previously, triggers on a SQLite3 table were silently dropped when the table was altered through operations that require table recreation (`remove_column`, `add_foreign_key`, `add_check_constraint`, or `add_column` with `null: false`). This happened because SQLite automatically drops triggers when the referenced table is dropped, and the `alter_table` method did not restore them afterward — unlike foreign keys and check constraints, which are already preserved.

This PR adds a `triggers(table_name)` method that queries `sqlite_master` and `sqlite_temp_master` for existing trigger definitions, and restores them after table recreation in `alter_table`.

Fixes #56810

items.title: Query unencrypted models on a non-main Ractor with extend_queries enabled
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

With `config.active_record.encryption.extend_queries` enabled, every `where`, `find` and `exists?` goes through `deterministic_encrypted_attributes`. It memoizes with `||=`, and for a model without encrypted attributes the result is `nil`, so each call writes the class instance variable. On a non-main Ractor that raises, even for a model already used on the main Ractor:

```
Ractor::IsolationError: can not set instance variables of classes/modules by non-main Ractors
```

So enabling that option makes all the queries of unencrypted models fail on a non-main Ractor. Measured in a production application after `ractorize!`, on Ruby 4.0.9 and SQLite, with the option enabled:

| On a non-main Ractor | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Model.find(id)` | `Ractor::IsolationError` | works |
| `Model.where(...).first` | `Ractor::IsolationError` | works |
| `Model.exists?(id)` | `Ractor::IsolationError` | works |

With the option disabled, which is the default, these worked already and still do.

### Detail

`deterministic_encrypted_attributes` now returns early when the model has no encrypted attributes, so it doesn't write anything. It still returns `nil`, which its callers expect.

This doesn't make models using `encrypts` work on a non-main Ractor. With or without this option they still raise, because their pending attribute decorators are not shareable. That is a separate issue.

items.title: dependent: :destroy_async on has_many :through destroys target record…
items.body:
Fixes #58564

### Motivation / Background

`dependent: :destroy_async` behaved differently from the synchronous deletion path on a `has_many :through` association.

The documented behavior for `:through` associations is that the **join records** are the ones removed, not the target records:

> If using with the `:through` option, the association on the join model must be a `belongs_to`, and the records which get deleted are the join records, rather than the associated records.
> — `ActiveRecord::Associations::ClassMethods#has_many`

> NOTE: The `:dependent` option is ignored with the `:through` option. When using `:through`, the join model must have a `belongs_to` association, and the deletion affects only the join records, not the associated records.
> — Active Record Associations guide

However, the asynchronous path collected the ids of the **target** records and enqueued them, so `ActiveRecord::DestroyAssociationAsyncJob` destroyed the targets themselves. With a shared target this silently deleted records still referenced by other owners, and ran their destroy callbacks.

```ruby
class Team < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :memberships
  has_many :users, through: :memberships, dependent: :destroy_async
end

user = User.create!
team_one = Team.create!
team_two = Team.create!
team_one.users << user
team_two.users << user

team_one.destroy!
# after the job runs

User.exists?(user.id)                              # => false  (before this PR)
Membership.exists?(team: team_two, user: user)     # => false  (before this PR)
```

The same scenario with `dependent: :destroy` only removes `team_one`'s membership, which is the behavior `:destroy_async` should match.

### Detail

`HasManyAssociation#handle_dependency` now resolves the records to enqueue and the reflection to enqueue them for through two overridable hooks instead of always using `load_target` and `reflection`:

* `destroy_async_records` — records whose ids get enqueued
* `destroy_async_reflection` — reflection providing the class the job instantiates

For a plain `has_many` these return `load_target` and `reflection`, so its behavior is unchanged.

`HasManyThroughAssociation` overrides both to target the join model. `destroy_async_records` builds the join-record scope with the exact same three lines already used by the synchronous `delete_records`:

```ruby
scope = through_association.scope
scope.where! construct_join_attributes(*records)
scope.where(through_scope_attributes)
```

Reusing `construct_join_attributes` and `through_scope_attributes` means association scopes, `:source_type` polymorphic joins, STI conditions and composite/custom primary keys are handled identically to the synchronous path. `destroy_async_reflection` returns `through_reflection`, so the job receives the join class and destroys join records — running their destroy callbacks, as `:destroy` does.

Batching via `destroy_association_async_batch_size` and the `:ensuring_owner_was` option keep working, now slicing join-record ids.

Existing tests in `destroy_association_async_test.rb` asserted the previous, undocumented behavior and were updated to assert the documented one: join records are destroyed and targets are left alone. The first test now uses a target shared by two owners so the regression from #58564 is covered directly.

### Additional information

This is a behavior change for applications relying on `dependent: :destroy_async` destroying target records on a `has_many :through`. That behavior contradicted both the documentation and the synchronous path, and could delete records shared with other owners. Applications that do want the targets destroyed can declare `dependent: :destroy_async` on the underlying `has_many` instead.

The issue was first reported to the Rails security team, which classified it as a non-security issue and directed it to the public tracker.

items.title: Fix SQLite3 data loss when altering tables inside a transaction
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes #55866. Fixes #58705. Follow-up to #55907.

On SQLite, column changes such as `remove_column`, `change_column_null` and `change_column_default` rebuild the table: copy it, drop the original, and recreate it. Rails turns foreign keys off around the rebuild, but SQLite ignores `PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF` inside a transaction, and migrations run inside one. So dropping the original table fires `ON DELETE CASCADE`, `SET NULL` and `SET DEFAULT` on the referencing tables, and their rows are silently deleted or set to `NULL`.

#55907 fixed this only when no transaction is open. `rename_column` no longer rebuilds the table on main, but the other column changes still do.

### Detail

When exactly one joinable transaction is open (as in `db:migrate`) and the table is referenced by such a foreign key, `alter_table` now:

1. commits the open transaction, so `PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF` takes effect,
2. rebuilds the table in its own transaction,
3. begins a new transaction for the rest of the migration.

If the rebuild fails, it is rolled back, foreign keys are turned back on, and the original error is raised.

Trade-off: in this case, changes made earlier in the same transaction are committed and are not rolled back if the migration fails later. Other tables are not affected. Nested and non-joinable transactions (for example, transactional tests) are left unchanged, because committing them is not safe.

### Additional information

The new tests in `sqlite3_adapter_test.rb` fail on main: the referencing row is deleted (`CASCADE`) or its foreign key is set to `NULL` (`SET NULL`). People in the comments report losing production data this way, for example with `change_column_null`.

items.title: Fix `distinct.count` for models with a composite primary key
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

`relation.distinct.count` raises `ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid` for any model
with a composite primary key. Runnable reproduction (from the bug report
templates):

```ruby
require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"
  gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main"
  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record"
require "minitest/autorun"

ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: ":memory:")

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :orders, primary_key: ["shop_id", "id"], force: true do |t|
    t.integer "shop_id", null: false
    t.integer "id", null: false
  end
end

class Order < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.primary_key = [:shop_id, :id]
end

class BugTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_distinct_count
    Order.create!(shop_id: 1, id: 1)
    assert_equal 1, Order.distinct.count
    # ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid: no such column: "shop_id", "id":
    #   SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT ["shop_id", "id"]) FROM "orders"
  end
end
```

Fixes #55401.

### Detail

**Cause:** when counting with `distinct` and `column_name == :all`,
`perform_calculation` swaps `:all` for the primary key to emit the cheaper
`COUNT(DISTINCT pk)` instead of a subquery
(`activerecord/lib/active_record/relation/calculations.rb:451`). That shortcut
predates composite primary key support: an Array primary key falls into
`aggregate_column`'s `else` branch and is stringified into a single
non-existent column name.

**Fix:** skip the single-column shortcut when the model has a composite
primary key. `column_name` then stays `:all`, and `build_count_subquery?`
routes the relation into the existing `build_count_subquery` path — whose own
comment notes that multi-column `COUNT DISTINCT` must go through a subquery.
This is the exact query shape CPK models already produce today when an
ORDER BY is present (`Order.order(:x).distinct.count` works on main). The
`model.composite_primary_key?` guard mirrors its existing uses in
`finder_methods.rb`. This also fixes `distinct.limit(n).count`, which raised
the same way through `build_count_subquery`.

Single-PK models take exactly the same code path as before.

### Additional information

- Supersedes #55432 (thanks @robzolkos for the earlier patch) — that approach
  added Array handling in `aggregate_column`/`operation_over_aggregate_column`
  plus a hand-rolled count-over-subquery; routing into the existing
  `build_count_subquery` needs only this one-line guard.
- `distinct.group(:x).count` on a CPK model also raises on main; it raises
  before and after this change and is deliberately out of scope (it needs
  separate handling in `execute_grouped_calculation`, and grouped distinct
  full-row counting is semantically `COUNT(*)` per group since primary keys
  are unique).
- Tests after rebasing onto current `main`: `test/cases/calculations_test.rb`
  on SQLite in-memory (239 runs, 664 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors); full
  Active Record suite on SQLite (9,849 runs, 35,110 assertions, 0 failures,

items.title: Upload tracked variants before publishing records
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

When a tracked variant is first processed, Active Storage currently publishes its variant record before uploading the image. A failed upload leaves a record that marks the variant as processed, preventing regeneration. Concurrent requests can also observe the record before its image is available.

Related to #55088.

### Detail

This change does not alter when variant processing starts: lazily processed variants are still generated on first use. Once processing begins—whether lazily, immediately, or in a background job—upload the image before creating or finding its variant record. The record therefore remains an availability marker for a successfully uploaded variant.

Delete uploaded files on transaction rollback, and defer enqueuing purge jobs for failed or unused blobs until the enclosing transaction commits.

Add regression tests for upload visibility, retry after failure, rollback cleanup, record creation failures, and deferred purging. A concurrency test uses two threads with separate SQLite connections and synchronization barriers to verify that both callers resolve to the same variant record and only the losing upload is purged.

items.title: Don't mark a serialized attribute changed when it was only encoded differently
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

`Type::Serialized#changed_in_place?` compares the stored bytes with a fresh encoding of the value. A row whose bytes the coder wouldn't produce today is therefore reported as changed as soon as the attribute is read, even though nothing was modified.

Since #58612 (99a9ba3fe5), that includes every `store` or `serialize coder: ActiveRecord::Coders::JSON` row containing `<`, `>` or `&` that was written before 8.1.4. Earlier versions wrote those characters HTML-escaped. Reproduced with the released gems on PostgreSQL:

```ruby
class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  store :settings, accessors: [:title], coder: ActiveRecord::Coders::JSON
end

# written by activerecord 8.1.3:   {"title":"Tom & Jerry <3"}
post = Post.first   # read by activerecord 8.1.4
post.title
post.changed?        # => true  (false on 8.1.3)
post.changed         # => ["settings"]
```

The same happens to JSON a database writes itself; `jsonb::text` yields `{"identified": true}`. It costs more than an extra write. Saving issues an UPDATE that touches `updated_at` and runs update callbacks. And `Attached::One#attach` defers saving a record that already has changes, so for an Active Storage blob whose metadata reads as changed, `blob.preview_image.attach(...)` never saves.

### Detail

When the stored and new bytes differ, `changed_in_place?` now re-encodes the stored value with the current coder before concluding it changed. A record counts as changed only if the bytes the coder would write now differ from what it would write for the stored value.

- Nothing changes when the bytes already match, so the common path does the same work as before.
- Differences the coder itself would write still count as changes. Hash key order still counts, so `test_changed_in_place_compare_serialized_representation` still passes, and so do `1` vs `1.0` and real mutations. The new tests pin both.
- No equality method on the deserialized object is involved, unlike the opt-in `comparable:` from 6a71a2ffea, so this is safe for any coder.

### Additional information

The new tests in `serialized_attribute_test.rb` and `blob_test.rb` fail without the change. Run locally:

- **SQLite:** `serialized_attribute_test`, `store_test`, `dirty_test`, `attribute_methods_test`, the coder, JSON and encryption tests. 660 runs, 0 failures.
- **PostgreSQL:** `serialized_attribute_test`, `dirty_test`, the JSON, hstore and encryption tests. 505 runs, 0 failures.
- **Active Storage:** `test/models`. 193 runs, 0 failures.

items.title: Action Cable fastlane broadcasts
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This PR introduces an optimization that significantly reduces Action Cable broadcasting latency by avoiding decoding-encoding every message for each client. The fastlane mode decodes/encodes once per identifier instead.

In addition to broadcasting latency improvement (which becomes impactful only at certain scale), this optimization reduces CPU usage and as a side effect reduce the number of out-of-order deliveries (though, can't eliminate them completely).

This optimization has been used in production for a while via [actioncable-next](https://github.com/anycable/actioncable-next) gem.

### Detail

A new Action Cable configuration parameter added, `config.action_cable.fastlane_broadcasts_enabled`. Defaults to  false but is set to true via `load_defaults 8.2`.

When enabled, it changes the way stream handler callbacks are generated: in case no user callback neither an explicit coder is provided, we use the most straightforward callback possible: just send the raw broadcast payload without decoding/encoding it. Almost: we still need to attach an identifier (for client-side routing) but that can be done once per identifier, not per client.

The once-per-identifier decoding is achieved by wrapping the broadcast payload into an _envelope struct_, Message. It quacks like a String (via `#to_str`, etc.), so the previous contract is satisfied (and we don't need to refactor, say, subscription adapters, built-in or third-party). It comes with the `#encoded_for(identifier)` method that caches a resulting identifier-specific payload during the first call (via Concurrent::Map).

#### Benchmarks

Using [action-cable-next-playground](https://github.com/anycable/action-cable-next-playground) setup (used for the original refactoring).

With fastlane mode on, **latency decreases by 1.5-2x** Here are example `websocket-bench` runs:

```
# fastlane=false
[2026-09-08T23:44:12+03:00] clients:   600    95per-rtt:  94ms    min-rtt:   1ms    median-rtt:  34ms    max-rtt: 127ms
[2026-09-08T23:44:15+03:00] clients:  1400    95per-rtt: 189ms    min-rtt:   1ms    median-rtt:  79ms    max-rtt: 253ms
[2026-09-08T23:44:23+03:00] clients:  2000    95per-rtt: 372ms    min-rtt:   1ms    median-rtt: 121ms    max-rtt: 472ms

# fastlane=true
[2026-09-08T23:45:08+03:00] clients:   600    95per-rtt:  77ms    min-rtt:   1ms    median-rtt:  23ms    max-rtt:  97ms
[2026-09-08T23:46:29+03:00] clients:  1400    95per-rtt: 157ms    min-rtt:   1ms    median-rtt:  52ms    max-rtt: 392ms
[2026-09-08T23:45:16+03:00] clients:  2000    95per-rtt: 219ms    min-rtt:   1ms    median-rtt:  79ms    max-rtt: 308ms
```

More benchmarks below: https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/58703#issuecomment-5597764373

#### JSON-only (which is fine)

The optimization only works for JSON payloads and is only activated if the `#stream_from` call has no user callback neither coder provided. This matches the current behaviour: even though we can specify a custom coder at broadacst time, the default stream handler always tries to parse the payload as JSON. Hence, custom-encoded broadcasts can only target stream handler with custom coders today; otherwise, JSON is implied.

### Additional information

This PR also increase `#stream_from` test coverage as well as adds missing (but years ago proposed) testing for `#stream_handler` and `#default_stream_handler` overrides (Closes https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/56505). The tests were added to ensure the optimization doesn't break the current behaviour.

items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because the Active Record Querying guide
says that, without a unique constraint, `create_or_find_by` "can raise
duplicate key violations". That is the opposite of what happens.

`create_or_find_by` tries the `INSERT` first and only falls back to a `SELECT`
when the insert fails with `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique`. Without a unique
constraint, the insert never fails, so no error is raised. Instead, a
duplicate row is silently created on every call. This is the more dangerous
failure mode, and the current wording hides it.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes the IMPORTANT note in the `create_or_find_by`
section of `guides/source/active_record_querying.md` to say that, without a
unique constraint, the insert never fails, so the method silently creates a
duplicate record instead of finding the existing one.

```ruby

User.where(email: "a@example.com").count      # => 2
```

items.title: Read by name for attributes whose slot moved after reset_column_information
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes #59831

Since #59141 the generated readers read by slot, and the slot is fixed when the reader is defined. A record loaded before `reset_column_information` keeps its old layout, so once the readers are defined again, a reader whose attribute moved to another slot reads the wrong value. In the issue, `user.name` returns the removed `legacy` column, and keeps returning it after `user.name = "changed"`, so a data migration could save the wrong value without an error.

### Detail

This follows the approach @seyhunak suggested in the issue, which keeps the read path unchanged. The model remembers the slot each attribute's reader was first defined with. When the readers are defined again, an attribute whose slot changed gets a reader that reads by name (the reader from before #59141), and every other attribute keeps reading by slot. Every record defines the attribute methods when it's initialized, so any layout a loaded record has is one the readers were defined with.

Slots move when a column is removed, and also when a column is added, since columns come before the attributes declared with `attribute` in the layout. Once an attribute has moved it keeps the by-name reader, even if it moves back to its first slot (a declared attribute after a column is added and then removed), because records from the layout in between may still be around.

Models whose schema isn't changed at runtime never get a by-name reader, and the slot reader is unchanged.

The regression tests in `hot_compatibility_test.rb` cover records loaded before a column is removed (read and write), before a column is added, with extra select columns, and declared attributes that move and move back. The teardown now also clears the model's cached columns, since a test that calls `reset_column_information` after removing a column would otherwise leave them stale for the next test.

### Additional information

Reads cost the same for models whose attributes don't move, since their generated reader is unchanged. On my machine with YJIT (5M reads, two runs each, the differences are noise):

| | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `record.name` | 65.2 to 69.9 ns | 64.2 to 64.8 ns |
| record loaded with `select("users.*, 1 AS one")` | 65.1 to 65.2 ns | 64.1 to 64.4 ns |

The full Active Record suite passes on SQLite. I couldn't run the Ractor suite locally: it fails to boot on `main` with Ruby 3.4 (`main_connection_handler` NameError in `RactorConnectionHandler`). The new state is only read and written while the attribute methods are being defined, like `@attribute_methods_generated`.

Fix insert_all raising "No unique index found for id" without unique_by
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes #56953

`insert_all` and `upsert_all` raise `ArgumentError: No unique index found for id` on PostgreSQL when `unique_by` is not provided, even on tables with a standard `id` primary key.

This affects libraries like SolidCable where `Model.insert(...)` (which uses `insert_all` with `on_duplicate: :skip`) fails on PostgreSQL.

**Root cause**: PostgreSQL's `indexes()` method explicitly excludes primary key indexes (`indisprimary = 'f'` in the SQL query). When `find_unique_index_for` can't find the PK in `unique_indexes` and `unique_by` is nil, it falls through to compare `model.primary_key` against `schema_cache.primary_keys(table_name)`. These two values are derived from different code paths and can diverge (composite PK where model overrides PK, multi-database setups with stale cache, etc.).

### Detail

When `unique_by` is nil and no matching unique index is found, `find_unique_index_for` now returns `nil` early. This is safe because:

- **`insert_all` (skip)**: generates `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` — valid SQL without a conflict target
- **`upsert_all` (update)**: `conflict_target` already falls back to `primary_keys` directly when `unique_by` is nil (line 275-276 of insert_all.rb)

The `match == primary_keys` branch is preserved for when `unique_by` IS explicitly provided and matches the PK columns (creates a synthetic IndexDefinition).

Tests updated:
- Added 7 new regression tests covering insert_all/upsert_all without unique_by on standard and composite PKs
- Updated existing composite PK test to run on all adapters (removed `!supports_insert_conflict_target?` skip)

items.title: [RF-DOCS] Rewrite and restructure the Action Cable Overview guide
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

A restructure and rewrite of the Action Cable Overview guide.

### Detail

Key changes:

* Restructure the flow of the guide to demonstrate end to end usage before drilling down into individual concepts.
* Add an intro section describing WebSockets and Pub/Sub.
* Add details about the architecture of Action Cable (server and pub/sub).
* Mention the recent adapterization of the server.
* Remove section on full-stack examples, instead integrating the info with the narrative flow.
* Describe the adapters in its own section.
* Add details on the `stream_from` and `stream_for` methods.

### Additional information

#### Internal Audit

- as app/channels are not generated in a new Rails app then we need some setup instructions and general introduction/overview at the start of this guide.
- Missing context in the first paragraph about why you might need to integrate websockets with your application (i.e. chat functionality seems like the most likely/common use-case).
- Section 3.2.3 is a repeat of section 3.1.2 - error handling. 
- Likewise 3.2.4 is a repeat of 3.1.3 - callbacks.
- The full-stack examples section - it's a good idea to include something like this, but there is so much code here that might be completely foreign to the reader. Maybe a separate tutorial/blog-style guide around implementing ActionCable would be better for this content, and keep the guide for reference/explanation only.
- Reading further, I can see that there's a link to more examples in section 6.3. I would maybe suggest that we remove the examples here and just move this link to further up the guide for readers to choose a walk through of how to implement the functionality upon following the link.

This was a bit of a funny one to think about with regards to beginners, because I think you wouldn't be trying to implement and understand lots of these concepts if you were a complete beginner - I think it's more intermediate-level functionality, once you have the basics down.

That said, I think the structure of this guide is the biggest thing we can think about where beginners are concerned. So, to imagine a beginner reading maybe the first few paragraphs with some broad concepts and explanations of terminology, and then perhaps having the option to follow a link to step through an implementation guide, that they may not understand all of at first, but can follow instructions. Then the more advanced reader can engage with the following sections, that include higher level concepts.

Maybe mention at the top that "Now that Hotwire is the default, the majority of apps won't need custom channels. And those that do can get the files back via the generator."

New Rails apps use [SolidCabl](https://github.com/rails/solid_cable)e by default instead of the async adapter (as mentioned in the Dependencies section).
I agree with Harriet that the structure of the guide can be improved for beginners. I'm wondering if it would be possible to integrate the fullstack examples in the other sections, instead of doing it separately. (this would be a lot of work though).
Should this guide explain broadcasting with Hotwire?

This guide starts with a lot of new concepts at once without showing any examples. I think it would be nice if we could start introducing concepts on-by-one with working code examples.

For example by first starting with just the ServerSide Components and using the browser console/debugger we can send messages to the server and see what responses we get back. After that we can introduce the client side.

Showing how this works will also help debugging ActionCable issues.

For example, if I start a new Rails app and add a channel:


items.title: Add `clobber:` option to `ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection`
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Refs #59028.

Since #58306 gave `HashConfig` value equality, `establish_connection` reuses
the existing connection pool for an equal configuration even when that
configuration was newly built. In Rails 8.1.4, an existing pool was reused
only when `establish_connection` resolved to the exact configuration object
that pool was established with, so passing a configuration hash, or an
environment name after rebuilding `configurations`, always established a new
pool. Code that relied on that, such as test setups that expect a fresh
SQLite `:memory:` database on each `establish_connection`, now gets the old
database back.

`ConnectionHandler#establish_connection` already accepts `clobber:` to skip
reuse, but `ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection` doesn't expose it, so
the only public way to force a new pool is to call `remove_connection` first.

### Detail

This Pull Request adds `clobber:` to `ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection`
and passes it through to the handler:

```ruby
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(
  { adapter: "sqlite3", database: ":memory:" },
  clobber: true
)
```

The default stays `clobber: false`, so main's pool-reuse behavior is
unchanged; the keyword lets callers be explicit about which behavior they
want.

To keep brace-less calls such as
`establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: ":memory:")` working, the
signature is `establish_connection(config_or_env = nil, clobber: false,
**config)`: remaining keywords are treated as the configuration, and passing
a configuration both positionally and as keywords raises `ArgumentError`.

### Additional information

#59028 also asks whether the new reuse is intended for configuration hashes.
If restoring the 8.1 behavior is preferred instead, this keyword is still
useful for being explicit, but I'm happy to rework or close this.

items.title: Fix preloader to respect case-insensitive column collations
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes #56780

When preloading associations where the key column has a case-insensitive collation (SQLite `NOCASE`, MySQL `_ci`, PostgreSQL `citext`), the database returns matching records but the preloader fails to associate them back to their owners. `owners_by_key` is a plain Ruby Hash with case-sensitive key lookup — `"Home"` and `"home"` are different keys in Ruby even though they match in the database.

### Detail

Add `Column#case_sensitive?` with adapter-specific overrides (SQLite: `NOCASE` collation; PostgreSQL: `citext` type and non-deterministic collations detected via the existing `column_definitions` query — zero extra DB round-trips). In the preloader, downcase string keys only when the flag is set — zero overhead on the common case-sensitive path.
